title: Query Invalidation
description: Learn how to invalidate and refetch queries after mutations to keep the cache fresh.

data.text: React Query keeps fetched data in a client-side cache. After a mutation changes server data, the cached version is now **stale** â€” it no longer reflects reality. **Query invalidation** marks affected cached queries as stale and triggers a refetch. This is the primary mechanism for keeping your UI in sync with the server.

terms.definition: A QueryClient method that marks matching cached queries as stale and schedules them to be refetched.
The state of cached data that may no longer be accurate and should be refetched before being shown.
The unique array-based identifier for a query in the cache, used to target specific queries for invalidation.
Re-executing the queryFn to replace stale cache data with fresh data from the server.

data.text: `invalidateQueries` accepts a flexible `queryKey` argument. You can target an exact query by passing the same key used in `useQuery`, use a prefix to invalidate a whole family of queries, or supply a `predicate` function for fine-grained control.

rows: Only the single user query is marked stale
All queries whose key starts with ['users'] are marked stale
Only successful queries matching the predicate are invalidated
Every cached query is invalidated â€” use carefully in large apps

data.text: The most common pattern is to invalidate in the `onSuccess` callback of a mutation. For mutations that affect a list (adding a comment to a post), you may need to invalidate both the list query and the individual item query. The order matters â€” invalidate the specific item query first, then the list.

data.title: Invalidating Multiple Related Queries
data.content: Using onSuccess to invalidate both a list and an individual resource after a mutation.

data.title: Granular Invalidation Keeps UI Smooth
data.text: Invalidate only the queries that actually changed. Invalidating everything triggers a burst of network requests that can slow down the app.

If you invalidate only in `onSuccess`, queries that failed to invalidate on error may never be refreshed. Moving invalidation to `onSettled` guarantees it runs regardless of whether the mutation succeeds or fails â€” a safer default for production apps.

data.title: onSettled Invalidation Pattern
data.content: Using onSettled to invalidate whether the mutation succeeds or fails.

data.text: Both `invalidateQueries` and `setQueryData` can update the cache after a mutation, but they serve different purposes. `invalidateQueries` is safer because it re-fetches from the server and guarantees data freshness. `setQueryData` is faster because it skips the network request but can diverge from the server if you get the update logic wrong.

cards.title: invalidateQueries
cards.description: Marks queries as stale and refetches from the server.

cards.title: setQueryData
cards.description: Directly patches the cache without a network request.
cons: Easy to get wrong if the patch logic is buggy

items.question: Does invalidation happen immediately or in the background?
items.answer: In React Query v5, invalidation marks queries as stale and triggers a background refetch. If the query is currently being displayed, it will update when the refetch resolves.

items.question: Can I invalidate queries from anywhere in my app?
items.answer: Yes, as long as you have access to the QueryClient instance. Pass it down via context, a hook, or a prop.

items.question: What if a query is not currently active?
items.answer: It is simply marked as stale in the cache. The next time it is fetched, React Query will refetch it before returning the data.

data.title: Exercise: Invalidate After Delete
data.description: Practice invalidating multiple query keys after a delete mutation.
steps: Create a useQuery that fetches a list of projects from /api/projects.
Create a DeleteProjectButton that calls DELETE /api/projects/:id using useMutation.
In onSettled, invalidate ['projects'] to refresh the list.
In onSuccess, also invalidate ['project', projectId] in case the detail view is open.
Add a predicate to only invalidate successful queries: predicate: (q) => q.state.status === 'success'.
Verify by deleting a project and watching both the list and any open detail view update.
data.expectedOutcome: After deleting a project, the list refreshes automatically. If the detail page is open for the deleted project, it also refetches and shows a not-found state.

data.caption: How query invalidation propagates through the cache and triggers refetch.
data.definition:
flowchart TB
    M[Mutation succeeds] --> I[invalidateQueries called]
    I --> S[Query marked as stale]
    S --> F{Query currently active?}
    F -->|Yes| R[Background refetch triggered]
    F -->|No| W[Wait for next subscriber]
    W --> R
    R --> U[Cache updated with fresh data]
    U --> C[UI re-renders automatically]

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: invalidateQueries marks matching cached queries as stale and schedules refetch
Call invalidation in onSuccess or onSettled after a mutation
Use queryKey prefixes to invalidate a family of queries at once
Use predicates for fine-grained control over which queries to refresh
Prefer invalidateQueries over setQueryData for most cases â€” safety over speed
data.takeaway: Query invalidation is the primary mechanism for keeping the cache consistent after data changes. Master it and your cache will rarely lie to your users.
